extraction.text:
Product Providers should remain and be ultimately responsible for the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement adopted and record keeping of ownership, regardless of any outsourcing arrangement1.
1 Given that these tokenised products are offered to the public in Hong Kong and the importance of maintaining proper records to reflect investors’ ownership, the Product Provider should remain fully responsible, despite any outsourcing arrangement such as those envisaged under 6.8 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds. For factors of consideration, please also refer to Part A of the Appendix to the Tokenised Securities Circular, where applicable, when formulating the tokenisation arrangement.
Product Providers should ensure that proper records of token holders’ ownership interests in the product are maintained and the tokenisation arrangement is operationally compatible with service providers involved2.
Product Providers should confirm and, upon SFC’s request, demonstrate to the SFC’s satisfaction the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, record keeping of ownership and the integrity of the smart contracts5.
5 Product Providers should confirm and demonstrate to the SFC that, at a minimum, they comply with the requirements as set out in paragraphs 10 to 13 above and the smart contracts are not subject to any contract vulnerabilities or security flaws with a high level of confidence.
Product Providers should, upon SFC’s request, obtain third party audit or verification on the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, record keeping of ownership and integrity of the smart contracts.
Product Providers should, upon SFC’s request, obtain satisfactory legal opinion to support its application.
6.8 The scheme, or in the case of a unit trust, the trustee or the person so appointed by the trustee must maintain a register of holders.
6.8 The scheme, or in the case of a unit trust, the trustee or the person so appointed by the trustee must maintain a register of holders. The Commission must be advised on request of the address(es) where the register is kept.
6.11C Where a third party is engaged in the valuation of a scheme, the management company shall exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence in the selection, appointment and ongoing monitoring of such third party in ensuring such entity possesses the appropriate level of knowledge, experience and resources that commensurate with the appropriate valuation policies and procedures for each scheme. The valuation activities of such third party should be subject to ongoing supervision and periodic review by the management company.
13. Where intermediaries issue (eg, fund managers of tokenised funds) or are substantially involved in the issuance of the Tokenised Securities which they intend to deal in or advise on, they remain responsible for the overall operation of the tokenisation arrangement notwithstanding any outsourcing to third-party vendors/service providers.
17. Where intermediaries deal in, advise on, or manage portfolios investing in Tokenised Securities, intermediaries are reminded to conduct due diligence on the issuers and their third-party vendors/service providers involved in the tokenisation arrangement as well as the features and risks arising from the tokenisation arrangement. 18. Intermediaries should understand and be satisfied with the controls implemented by the issuers and their third-party vendors/service providers to manage ownership and technology risks of the Tokenised Securities before they engage in related activities. Please refer to Parts A and B of the Appendix to this circular for a non-exhaustive list of factors for consideration.

findings.details: The supplied material establishes normative propositions, not facts about any Product Provider's compliance. No conclusion of fulfilment follows from the source text alone.

Allocation of authority and responsibility, supervisory conduct, and operational or record-keeping outcomes require separate assessment. Governance and delegation terms could evidence retained authority; selection, monitoring and remediation records could evidence supervision; actual operational performance and ownership records could evidence outcomes. These are evidentiary categories, not an exhaustive checklist imposed by the excerpts.

Paragraph 10 and footnote 1 support a non-transferable-accountability reading. Their references to soundness and record keeping, reinforced by the express ensure wording in the ownership-record provision, also support substantive performance expectations. The packet does not settle whether any particular operational failure necessarily establishes breach or whether adequate conduct can suffice under an applicable standard.

Neither nominal retention of authority nor good outcomes alone conclusively establishes fulfilment. An applicable standard and facts about actual authority, supervision, operations and records remain necessary; the excerpts do not specify their sufficient combination.

Paragraph 14's punctuation supports an unconditional confirmation requirement and request-triggered demonstration. Footnote 5 can be harmonised as defining the minimum content of those acts while preserving that trigger, but its unqualified confirmation-and-demonstration wording supports a rival broader reading. The packet does not conclusively resolve the tension.

The SFC-satisfaction standard most directly attaches to demonstration in paragraph 14. Footnote 5 adds minimum compliance and smart-contract assurance content; whether high confidence qualifies only the smart-contract proposition or the whole minimum showing remains uncertain. Neither standard supplies a quantified threshold.

No request means paragraphs 15 and 16 do not themselves trigger obtaining an audit or verification or a legal opinion. It does not establish compliance, SFC satisfaction, or an exemption from substantive requirements. No actual request history is supplied.

The complete applicable text of 26EC22 paragraphs 10–13, missing footnote 2, relevant Appendix factors, actor definitions and application facts are needed to resolve remaining scope and sufficiency questions. No separate question or concern identity table was supplied.

findings.details: No actual outsourcing contracts, allocations of authority, oversight records, operational evidence, ownership records, smart-contract assessments, confirmation communications or SFC requests are supplied. No finding of fulfillment or breach can therefore be made.

A defensible assessment must distinguish retained accountability and supporting authority arrangements, supervisory conduct in practice, and operational and ownership-record outcomes. Evidence of one category alone does not establish the other categories. The excerpts do not specify which powers must be retained or a complete sufficiency test.

Paragraph 10 supports both an emphasis on non-transferable accountability and a broader reading requiring substantive discharge of responsibility for soundness and records. It does not resolve whether particular failures establish noncompliance irrespective of care, or whether an applicable conduct standard governs fulfillment. Neither a strict outcome guarantee nor a reasonable-care safe harbour is established.

Section 6.11C expressly supplies a care and supervision standard for outsourced valuation. Its standard cannot automatically be transferred to tokenisation; any application or analogy requires justification.

Paragraph 14 most naturally conditions demonstration alone on request. Footnote 5's unqualified wording creates a rival reading concerning demonstration, while also clarifying the recipient and minimum content. The scope of SFC satisfaction over confirmation and the scope of the high-confidence qualifier remain interpretive questions.

No SFC request does not establish approval, satisfaction, absence of vulnerabilities or compliance. It leaves underlying responsibility and the ordinary reading of the confirmation requirement intact.

The full applicable 26EC22 instrument, paragraphs 10–13, footnote 2 and incorporated Appendix factors are unavailable. The packet does not establish instrument versions, complete definitions or applicability to a particular entity or product.

Paragraphs 15 and 16 specify different request-triggered deliverables: technical or operational third-party assurance and a satisfactory legal opinion supporting the application. Neither is stated to substitute for the other or automatically discharge paragraph 14.

The supplied intermediary paragraph 13 belongs to a separately described intermediary context; matching paragraph numbers do not establish that it satisfies footnote 5's incorporation of paragraphs 10–13.

residual_questions.details: The supplied material establishes normative propositions, not facts about any Product Provider's compliance. No conclusion of fulfilment follows from the source text alone.

Allocation of authority and responsibility, supervisory conduct, and operational or record-keeping outcomes require separate assessment. Governance and delegation terms could evidence retained authority; selection, monitoring and remediation records could evidence supervision; actual operational performance and ownership records could evidence outcomes. These are evidentiary categories, not an exhaustive checklist imposed by the excerpts.

Paragraph 10 and footnote 1 support a non-transferable-accountability reading. Their references to soundness and record keeping, reinforced by the express ensure wording in the ownership-record provision, also support substantive performance expectations. The packet does not settle whether any particular operational failure necessarily establishes breach or whether adequate conduct can suffice under an applicable standard.

Neither nominal retention of authority nor good outcomes alone conclusively establishes fulfilment. An applicable standard and facts about actual authority, supervision, operations and records remain necessary; the excerpts do not specify their sufficient combination.

Paragraph 14's punctuation supports an unconditional confirmation requirement and request-triggered demonstration. Footnote 5 can be harmonised as defining the minimum content of those acts while preserving that trigger, but its unqualified confirmation-and-demonstration wording supports a rival broader reading. The packet does not conclusively resolve the tension.

The SFC-satisfaction standard most directly attaches to demonstration in paragraph 14. Footnote 5 adds minimum compliance and smart-contract assurance content; whether high confidence qualifies only the smart-contract proposition or the whole minimum showing remains uncertain. Neither standard supplies a quantified threshold.

No request means paragraphs 15 and 16 do not themselves trigger obtaining an audit or verification or a legal opinion. It does not establish compliance, SFC satisfaction, or an exemption from substantive requirements. No actual request history is supplied.

residual_questions.details: No actual outsourcing contracts, allocations of authority, oversight records, operational evidence, ownership records, smart-contract assessments, confirmation communications or SFC requests are supplied. No finding of fulfillment or breach can therefore be made.

A defensible assessment must distinguish retained accountability and supporting authority arrangements, supervisory conduct in practice, and operational and ownership-record outcomes. Evidence of one category alone does not establish the other categories. The excerpts do not specify which powers must be retained or a complete sufficiency test.

Paragraph 10 supports both an emphasis on non-transferable accountability and a broader reading requiring substantive discharge of responsibility for soundness and records. It does not resolve whether particular failures establish noncompliance irrespective of care, or whether an applicable conduct standard governs fulfillment. Neither a strict outcome guarantee nor a reasonable-care safe harbour is established.

Section 6.11C expressly supplies a care and supervision standard for outsourced valuation. Its standard cannot automatically be transferred to tokenisation; any application or analogy requires justification.

Paragraph 14 most naturally conditions demonstration alone on request. Footnote 5's unqualified wording creates a rival reading concerning demonstration, while also clarifying the recipient and minimum content. The scope of SFC satisfaction over confirmation and the scope of the high-confidence qualifier remain interpretive questions.

No SFC request does not establish approval, satisfaction, absence of vulnerabilities or compliance. It leaves underlying responsibility and the ordinary reading of the confirmation requirement intact.

The full applicable 26EC22 instrument, paragraphs 10–13, footnote 2 and incorporated Appendix factors are unavailable. The packet does not establish instrument versions, complete definitions or applicability to a particular entity or product.

Paragraphs 15 and 16 specify different request-triggered deliverables: technical or operational third-party assurance and a satisfactory legal opinion supporting the application. Neither is stated to substitute for the other or automatically discharge paragraph 14.

The supplied intermediary paragraph 13 belongs to a separately described intermediary context; matching paragraph numbers do not establish that it satisfies footnote 5's incorporation of paragraphs 10–13.
